newsitem.title: UK: UK industry wants tight budget, wider Europe debate.
newsitem.headline: UK industry wants tight budget, wider Europe debate.

text.p: British industry leaders are hoping for a tight budget and a widening of the debate over Europe, Confederation of British Industry director-general Adair Turner said on Friday.
The CBI -- Britain's top industry group -- holds its annual conference next week. A host of leading politicians and captains of industry will attend.

Turner told Reuters that British industry was hoping for a prudent budget from Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke on November 26, so that the pressure to raise interest rates further, diminishes.
"We are now strongly in favour of a tight budget which will minimise the need for further rate rises and therefore not push the pound higher still," he said.
The pound has shot up by about nine percent on a trade-weighted basis since early August and British exporters are starting to squeal about their prices being forced up.
"We are concerned that if sterling keeps rising it will start to hurt export performance," Turner said.
With a buoyant domestic economy, fuelled by free-spending consumers, the lagging part of the British economy is the manufacturing sector, and exports in particular.

Another interest rate rise would probably force the pound higher still, squeezing exports further. And monetary tightening may be less effective than tax rises in restraining high street spending, particularly since last week's surprise quarter-point rate rise was not matched by British mortgage lenders.
"We certainly do not want a loose fiscal policy combined with a tight monetary policy. That would be precisely the wrong mix," Turner said.
The CBI conference, which takes place in Harrogate, Yorkshire on Monday and Tuesday, will debate the British economy on Tuesday morning.

Bank of England Governor Eddie George will also speak and may shed some light on monetary policy. In its quarterly inflation report, released on Wednesday, the Bank said interest rates would probably have to head higher in due course.
The conference will also hear from a number of politicians from both major political parties.
From the government, defence secretary Michael Portillo, Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine and foreign secretary Malcolm Rifkind will address the conference.
Taking up the cudgels for the opposition Labour Party will be shadow finance spokesman Gordon Brown and trade and industry spokeswoman Margaret Beckett.

Turner said the CBI would stay studiously neutral on the political front, in the run up to elections which must be held be May 1997. "We will comment on individual policies but we will not make overall political endorsements for any party."

One of the major themes of this year's conference will be Europe and a single European currency. Turner said the CBI will release on Sunday a major survey on attitudes to Europe and European Economic and Monetary Union.
The survey has been conducted in conjunction with the British Chambers of Commerce and the polling group MORI.
Two debates on Europe follow on Tuesday.

"We hope this will kick off a more economic, less political debate about EMU," Turner said. "At the moment, the CBI policy is to keep the options open but there will come a point next year, when we have to start coming off the fence."
From the pro-European camp, European Union Trade Commissioner Leon Brittan and Mario Monti, the European Commissioner responsible for the internal market, will attend the conference.
On the other side of the fence Conservative member of parliament and noted Eurosceptic, John Redwood, will be there.
